issues.description: The Comparative Fit Index (CFI) is reported as .86, which is well below the conventionally accepted threshold of .90 or .95 for acceptable model fit. This suggests the proposed model does not adequately represent the underlying data structure.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86)

issues.description: The study uses a standard Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CLPM), which is known to conflate between-person variance and within-person variance. This often leads to spurious or inflated cross-lagged effects. A Random Intercepts CLPM (RI-CLPM) would be required to make the causal claims suggested.
issues.quote: The autoregressive cross-lagged panel model allows examination of reciprocal influences among the three variables

issues.description: The authors use strong causal language ('influence', 'leads to', 'causal pathway') despite the data being purely observational and correlational. Cross-lagged models establish temporal precedence, not causality.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: One of the RWA items was missing at Time 2. This introduces measurement non-invariance across time points, potentially biasing the longitudinal estimates for the RWA factor.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government... was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: Environmentalism is operationalized using only two items focused on 'willingness to sacrifice.' This is a narrow subset of environmentalism and may not capture broader constructs like environmental concern, belief in climate change, or actual pro-environmental behavior.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual’s willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] two items on sacrifice intentions

issues.description: The internal consistency (reliability) for SDO (.69) and RWA (.70) is at the absolute lower bound of acceptability, especially for a large-scale study. This increases measurement error and attenuates the observed relationships.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used

issues.description: The model does not include any demographic or socioeconomic controls (e.g., income, education, political affiliation). These variables are known to correlate with both ideology and environmentalism and could be the true drivers of the observed associations.
issues.quote: The model thus included three latent variables across five measurement points, where each variable within a time point was set to predict each variable in the subsequent time point.

issues.description: The authors imposed a stationary model (constraining paths to be equal across all time points) without reporting a statistical test (e.g., a chi-square difference test) to determine if the relationships actually remained stable over the five-year period.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The manuscript fails to report the attrition rate or the number of participants who provided data at all five time points. In a 5-year longitudinal study, dropout is a significant concern for bias.
issues.quote: Of the 22,974 participants included in this study, the average age was 43 years at Time 1

issues.description: The sample is 86% Pākehā (New Zealand European), which over-represents the European population and may limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader, multi-ethnic New Zealand population or other cultures.
issues.quote: the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European).

issues.description: The authors compare the 'strength' of SDO vs RWA as predictors using unstandardized coefficients. Unless the latent variables have identical variances, unstandardized coefficients cannot be directly compared to determine which predictor is 'stronger'.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11... than RWA (B = -.02...)

issues.description: The discussion links the findings to 'speciesism' and 'environmental racism,' but the study did not measure attitudes toward animals or racial groups in an environmental context. This is an over-extrapolation of the 'willingness to sacrifice' measure.
issues.quote: This finding is analagous to Dhont et al.’s [32] research, which shows that prejudice towards non-human animals shares the same ideological underpinnings of prejudice towards social groups

issues.description: The authors used Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) for missing data but did not provide evidence that the data met the 'Missing at Random' (MAR) assumption, which is critical for FIML validity.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.description: The abstract claims a 'national probability sample,' but the methods section describes it as 'nationally representative.' These are distinct concepts (sampling method vs. sample characteristics).
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA... in a national probability sample over five years.

issues.description: The full wording for all items in the SDO and RWA scales is not provided, only examples. This prevents full evaluation of the content validity of the shortened scales used.
issues.quote: Three items favoured dominance, such as “To get ahead in life, it is sometimes okay to step on other groups”

issues.description: The cross-lagged effect of RWA on environmentalism (B = -.02) and the effect of environmentalism on RWA (B = -.01) are extremely small. In a sample of N=22,000, these reach significance despite being practically negligible.

The study uses the SDO-6 scale. The field has largely moved to SDO-7, which better distinguishes between SDO-Dominance and SDO-Egalitarianism, a distinction the authors themselves mention as important in the discussion.
issues.quote: Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] SDO6 scale.

issues.description: The authors state syntax will be available 'upon acceptance.' Scientific transparency requires that analytic code be available during the peer-review process to verify the model specifications.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The results section uses '2(1)' to report chi-square difference tests, which is likely a typographical error for 'Δχ²(1)'.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides significantly better fit to the data 2(1) = 50.98, p < .001

issues.description: The study measures 'willingness' (intentions) but discusses the results as if they explain 'environmental exploitation' (behavior). The intention-behavior gap is a well-documented issue in environmental psychology.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance
